_comment: THE ACCEPT VOCABULARY, STATED ONCE. `.github/scripts/accepted-findings.py` reads
this file to decide which review findings a dispatch acts on, and the
contributor docs (.claude/rules/worktree-delivery.md, CONTRIBUTING.md) point
here rather than restating it. What decides that code will be written to a
branch may not be a judgement call, so it is a LIST matched by a program —
never a classifier reading whether the conversation sounded agreeable.
THE MATCHING RULE: the reply's WHOLE text, trimmed of surrounding whitespace
and of trailing punctuation (. ! ,), compared case-insensitively against
`accept`. Nothing else counts. A reply that quotes a phrase inside a longer
sentence, asks a question, argues, or agrees in other words is NOT an
acceptance, and the thread and the code are left exactly as they are.
`dispatch` is the pull-request comment that starts one run over everything
accepted. It is a TRIGGER: the work list is derived from the threads, and
no other text in the dispatch comment is read.
`approve_label` is CHANGE-LEVEL consent (`conveyor:fix`, renamed from
`autofix`), a LABEL rather than a matched phrase like `accept` — the same
shape as `implement_label`, `run_label`, `archive_label` and
`keep_going_label` below. Placed on a
pull request, it means every finding the review raises there — now and
after every later push — is accepted without a reply in its thread, and the
analysis service's open issues join the work list beside them. Who may
place it is the same gate as a dispatch: write access, read from the label
event's sender; a label placed by anyone else is removed with a visible
comment. WITHOUT the label nothing changes: per-thread `accept` and the
`dispatch` comment are the only consent, exactly as before.
`dispute_marker` is the line the landing step writes at the top of a reply
when the fixing step DISPUTED a finding instead of fixing it. A later round
skips a thread carrying it (never disputed twice), and the archive guard
refuses an archive while a thread carrying it has no later comment by a
person. `round_marker` prefixes the landing step's own comments so rounds
can be counted from the pull request rather than from a store. Both
renamed from `autofix:disputed` / `autofix:round` alongside the label —
an HTML comment tag nobody reads is still part of the retired vocabulary
if it names the retired word.
`implement_label` and `run_label` are ISSUE-level consent, and they are the
only two entries here placed on an issue rather than a pull request.
`.github/scripts/remote-implement.py` fires on either, reads the
`issues: labeled` event, checks the labeller may push here (the
collaborators API, as the label gate does — a label event carries no
`author_association`), and fires one remote session for the issue's NUMBER;
placed by anyone else it is removed with a visible comment. The session
opens its pull request carrying NO label at all: a program — never the
session — carries the issue's grant forward once the pull request exists.
See .claude/rules/remote-session.md and .claude/rules/worktree-delivery.md.
THE FIVE `conveyor:` LABELS ARE ONE VOCABULARY, READ ONE WAY: A PROGRAM MAY
CARRY A GRANT FORWARD OR CONSUME ONE. IT MAY NEVER MINT ONE. Every label
here that authorises unattended work is placed by a person whose write
access the platform confirms at the moment it is acted on — directly, or
carried forward by `.github/scripts/carry-grant.py` recording whose
instruction it relayed. An automated session places none of them, ever.
`run_label` (`conveyor:run`) is a STANDING INSTRUCTION on the issue, read
at EVERY transition rather than recorded at the first. It means: implement
this, drive its pull request to mergeable, and archive it once merged —
the whole line for whichever LANE the issue is on (opsx: three stations;
plain: two, ending at the merge). Removing it halts the line at the next
station; work already running finishes.
`implement_label` (`conveyor:implement`), `approve_label` (`conveyor:fix`)
and `archive_label` (`conveyor:archive`) are the SINGLE-STATION labels —
what a person places to drive one station by hand, and what a workflow
places when carrying `conveyor:run` forward, so a station has one meaning
whoever placed its label.
`keep_going_label` (`conveyor:keep-going`) grants another `max_rounds` set
of unattended fixing rounds to a loop that stopped on the cap — placing
it also RE-TRIGGERS the workflow (the same `pull_request: labeled` event
`approve_label` uses), because a labelling event is what starts a round
at all. It is CONSUMED, and ONLY when it takes effect: the landing job
posts one `grant_marker` comment the moment a round actually lands past
the cap already in force, extends the effective cap by another
`max_rounds`, and removes the label — a round already under the
existing cap consumes nothing, so the grant is never spent early.
Placing it again after a later cap is a fresh judgement made with newer
evidence.
`max_rounds` is the loop's bound, a named constant read here rather than
buried in a workflow's `env`, default 5. Five rather than three because a
bound of three was measured stopping a loop mid-progress (#198: four
rounds produced 14, 10, 8 then 1 finding, nearly all new each round).
